newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland Loyalists issue death threat over march.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland Loyalists issue death threat over march.

text.p: Outlawed Protestant extremists threatened on Wednesday to kill Irish Catholics if Britain bans a controversial parade by pro-British Protestants in Northern Ireland next Sunday.

The Loyalist Volunteer Force (LVF) threatened to carry out the murders in the neighbouring Irish Republic if the march of the ancient Orange Order is not allowed to proceed through Garvaghy Road, a minority Catholic nationalist enclave in the town of Portadown.

"If the Orange parade does not go down the Garvaghy Road on Sunday, the Irish government may expect civilians to be killed in the Irish Republic," a male caller using a recognised LVF codeword said in a telephoned statement to Downtown radio station near Belfast.
"This threat will be carried out immediately if the parade is banned."

The LVF, a renegade guerrilla group that broke away earlier this year from groups controlled by the main Loyalist command, was banned last month by the British government because it was suspected of carrying out bombings and shootings.
The LVF statement accused the Irish government of interfering in the internal affairs of Northern Ireland, which is a province of Britain.
On Tuesday, Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern and his Foreign Minister Ray Burke, on a rare visit to Belfast, urged Britain not to allow the contentious march.
Catholic residents say they feel intimidated by what they portray as an annual display of pro-British superiority by the Orange Order. They plan a counter-demonstration.
The Order, an exclusively Protestant brotherhood which holds hundreds of processions across the province each summer, is a lawful body which condemns violence.
It says the Portadown parade will be a dignified event to celebrate its members' religious faith.
"Once and for all the Irish government has to learn that they'll not interfere in the internal affairs of Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom," the LVF statement said.
The Irish ministers signalled they opposed Britain using troops and police to push the march through the enclave in the face of nationalist opposition.
Ahern plans to discuss the march when he meets Prime Minister Tony Blair in London on Thursday. It will be their first official talks since each came to power recently.
Last year the British authorities banned the annual Orange Portadown parade. But Protestants rioted and brought the province to a virtual standstill.

The police reversed their decision after four days and allowed the Orangmen through. Catholics reacted furiously saying Britain had caved in to mob rule. Catholic rioters fought vicious street battles with police.
Britain has not yet announced a decision on this year's parade. On Tuesday Mo Mowlam, Northern Ireland Secretary, said she hoped for a compromise between the Orangemen and the Catholics
Earlier, Gerry Adams, leader of the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein, joined the Irish demands that Britain should not allow the parade to pass through through Catholic areas.

Adams, whose Irish Republican Army ally refuses to end guerrilla hostilities against British rule in Northern Ireland, said Sinn Fein upheld the right of the majority Protestant community and its marching groups to assert their sense of identity and culture.
"But they do not have the right to parade through nationalist areas where that presence is offensive," he said in an article about the province's stalled peace process in Belfast's Irish News daily.
